The frequency of a vibrating stretched wire is given by $f = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, where $L$ is the wire length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density. For resonance with the same tuning fork, $f$ remains constant, and $\mu$ is unchanged.

The tension $T$ equals the weight of the hanging mass, so $T = mg$. At the poles, $g$ is unchanged, but at the equator, the effective gravity is reduced to $g - R\omega^2$, where $R$ is Earth's radius and $\omega$ is its angular velocity. Consequently, $T_{\text{equator}} = m(g - R\omega^2) < T_{\text{pole}} = mg$.

Since $f \propto \frac{1}{L}\sqrt{T}$ and $f$ is constant, $L \propto \sqrt{T}$. With $T_{\text{equator}} < T_{\text{pole}}$, it follows that $\sqrt{T_{\text{equator}}} < \sqrt{T_{\text{pole}}}$, so $L_{\text{equator}} < L_{\text{pole}}$ to maintain the same frequency.

Thus, the vibrating length must be decreased, and the correct choice is $\boxed{A}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 258 Hz are sounded together. The time interval between two consecutive maxima is
questions.solution:
When two tuning forks of frequencies $256 \text{ Hz}$ and $258 \text{ Hz}$ are sounded together, the time interval between consecutive maxima corresponds to the beat period.

The beat frequency is given by the absolute difference: $f_{\text{beat}} = |256 - 258| = 2 \text{ Hz}$.

Therefore, the beat period is $T_{\text{beat}} = \frac{1}{f_{\text{beat}}} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 \text{ s}$.

The correct option is D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a source emitting waves of frequency 'F' moves towards an observer with a velocity $\frac{V}{3}$ and the observer moves away from the source with a velocity $\frac{\mathrm{V}}{4}$, the apparent frequency as heard by the observer will be ( $\mathrm{V}=$ velocity of sound)
questions.solution:
Apparent frequency for Doppler effect in sound

The apparent frequency $F'$ follows the formula $F' = F \left( \frac{V \pm v_o}{V \mp v_s} \right), where $F$ is the source frequency, $V$ is the speed of sound, $v_o$ is the observer velocity, and $v_s$ is the source velocity.

Sign conventions determine the operator: observer moving away uses $V - v_o$ in numerator, source moving toward uses $V - v_s$ in denominator.

Given $v_s = $\frac{V}{3} (toward observer) and $v_o = $\frac{V}{4} (away from source), we substitute:

$F' = F $\left( \frac{V - \frac{V}{4}}{V - \frac{V}{3}} \right) = F \left( \frac{\frac{3V}{4}}{\frac{2V}{3}} \right)$

Simplifying the complex fraction:

$F' = F \left( \frac{3V}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{2V} \right) = F \cdot \frac{9}{8}$

The apparent frequency is $\frac{9}{8}F$, corresponding to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two sound waves travelling in $the same direction have displacement
\begin{aligned}
& y_1=a \sin (0 \cdot 2 \pi x-50 \pi t) \text{$ and $} \\
& y_2=a \sin (0 \cdot 15 \pi x-46 \pi t)
\end{aligned}$
How many times, a listener can hear sound of maximum intensity in one second?
questions.solution:
The given displacement equations for the sound waves are $y_1 = a \sin (0.2\pi x - 50\pi t)$ and $y_2 = a \sin (0.15\pi x - 46\pi t)$.

From the general form $y = A \sin (kx - \omega t)$, we identify $\omega_1 = 50\pi$ and $\omega_2 = 46\pi$.

Using $\omega = 2\pi f$, we find $f_1 = \frac{50\pi}{2\pi} = 25$ Hz and $f_2 = \frac{46\pi}{2\pi} = 23$ Hz.

The beat frequency is given by $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2| = |25 - 23| = 2$ Hz.

This corresponds to 2 intensity maxima per second.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An open organ pipe is closed such that the third overtone of the closed pipe is found to be higher in frequency by 200 Hz than the second overtone of the original pipe. The fundamental frequency of the open pipe is (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Let $L$ be the length of the organ pipe and $v$ the speed of sound in air. For an open organ pipe, the fundamental frequency is $f_o = \frac{v}{2L}$, with overtones at integer multiples. The second overtone is $3f_o$.

When closed, the pipe behaves as a closed organ pipe with fundamental frequency $f_c = \frac{v}{4L}$, producing odd harmonics. The third overtone is $7f_c$.

Given that the closed pipe's third overtone exceeds the open pipe's second overtone by 200 Hz:

$7f_c = 3f_o + 200$

Since $f_c = \frac{1}{2}f_o$, substitution yields:

$\frac{7}{2}f_o = 3f_o + 200$

Solving for $f_o$:

$\frac{1}{2}f_o = 200$

$f_o = 400$

Fundamental frequency: $\boxed{400\text{ Hz}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of sonometer wire is ' $n$ '. If the tension and length are increased 3 times and diameter is increased twice, the new frequency will be
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a sonometer wire is given by $n = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, where $L$ is the length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density. Expressing $\mu$ in terms of material density $\rho$ and diameter $d$, we have $\mu = \rho \left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}\right).

Substituting yields $ n = $\frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{\rho \pi d^2}} = \frac{1}{Ld} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho \pi}}, establishing the proportionality $ n \propto $\frac{1}{Ld} \sqrt{T}.

With the new parameters $ L' = 3L$, $T' = 3T$, and $d' = 2d$, the frequency ratio becomes:

\frac{n'}{n} = \frac{Ld}{L'd'} \sqrt{\frac{T'}{T}} = \frac{Ld}{(3L)(2d)} \sqrt{\frac{3T}{T}} = \frac{1}{6} \sqrt{3}

Thus $ n' = $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$ n = $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$ n$, which corresponds to option C.

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical straight wires are stretched so as to produce 6 beats per second when vibrating simultaneously with tensions ' $\mathrm{T}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{T}_2$ ' respectively. On changing the tension slightly in one of them, the beat frequency remains unchanged. This will happen when (Given $\rightarrow \mathrm{T}_1 > \mathrm{T}_2$ )
questions.solution:
Problem Analysis: Given two identical wires with initial tensions $T_1 > T_2$, the frequencies satisfy $f_1 = C \sqrt{T_1}$ and $f_2 = C \sqrt{T_2}$, where $C$ is a constant. The 6 Hz beat frequency implies $f_1 - f_2 = 6$.

Altering tension slightly while maintaining the beat frequency at 6 Hz implies a crossover in frequencies. If $T_1$ is changed, the frequency must decrease such that $f_1' = f_2 - 6$, requiring $T_1$ to be decreased. If $T_2$ is changed, the frequency must increase such that $f_2' = f_1 + 6$, requiring $T_2$ to be increased.

The only consistent option is to decrease $T_1$ or increase $T_2$, matching choice D. The specific tension change magnitude (144) is irrelevant as only direction matters for the beat frequency to remain unchanged. The correct option is $\boxed{D}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with a velocity of one fifth of the velocity of sound. The percentage increase in the apparent frequency is
questions.solution:
Doppler effect for observer moving toward stationary source: apparent frequency $f' = f \left( \frac{v + v_o}{v} \right), where $ f$ is source frequency, $v$ is sound velocity, and $v_o$ is observer velocity.

Given observer velocity $v_o = $\frac{v}{5}, substitute$ to obtain:

f' = f $\left( \frac{v + \frac{v}{5}}{v} \right) =$ f $\left( \frac{\frac{6v}{5}}{v} \right) = \frac{6}{5}$ f = 1.2f$

The percentage increase is:

\frac{f' - f}{f} \times100\% = \frac{1.2f - f}{f} \times100\% = 0.2 \times100\% = 20\%$

The apparent frequency increases by $\boxed{20\%}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two tuning forks when sounded together produce 4 beats per second. One of the forks is in unison with 23 cm length of sonometer wire and other with 24 cm length of the same wire. The frequencies of the two tuning forks are
questions.solution:
Beat frequency analysis
The production of 4 beats per second indicates that the frequencies differ by 4 Hz: $|f_1 - f_2| = 4$.

Length-frequency relationship
For a sonometer wire under constant tension, frequency is inversely proportional to length: $f \propto 1/L$. Given lengths 23 cm and 24 cm: $f_1 \cdot 23 = f_2 \cdot 24$. Since 23 cm < 24 cm, the corresponding frequency must be higher: $f_1 > f_2$.

Solving the system
From the beat frequency: $f_1 = f_2 + 4$. Substituting into the length relation: $23(f_2 + 4) = 24f_2$, which simplifies to $23f_2 + 92 = 24f_2$, yielding $f_2 = 92$ Hz. Then $f_1 = 92 + 4 = 96$ Hz.

The frequencies are 96 Hz and 92 Hz, corresponding to $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pipe open at both ends produces a fundamental frequency $n_1$. When the pipe is kept with $\frac{3}{4}^{\text{th }}$ of its length in water, it produces a note of fundamental frequency $n_2$. The ratio of $\frac{n_1}{n_2}$ is
questions.solution:
A pipe of length $L$ has fundamental frequency $n_1 = \frac{v}{2L}$ when open at both ends.

When $\frac{3}{4}$ of the pipe is submerged in water, the remaining $\frac{1}{4}L$ length of air column behaves as a closed pipe, with fundamental frequency $n_2 = \frac{v}{4 \cdot \frac{1}{4}L} = \frac{v}{L}$.

The ratio of frequencies is therefore $\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{\frac{v}{2L}}{\frac{v}{L}} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a pipe closed at one end, air column is vibrating in its second overtone. The column has
questions.solution:
Nodes and Antinodes in a Pipe Closed at One End

A pipe closed at one end supports standing waves with a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Only odd harmonics are present in such systems.

The second overtone corresponds to the fifth harmonic, $n = 5$. The wavelength satisfies $L = 5\lambda/4$, and the standing wave pattern consists of three nodes and three antinodes.

Among the options, $\boxed{A}$ identifies this configuration correctly.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of a sonometer wire is 50 Hz for some length and tension. If the length is increased by $25 \%$ by keeping tension same then frequency change of second harmonic is
questions.solution:
50 Hz, increasing the length by 25% gives $L_2 = \frac{5}{4}L_1$. Since tension and linear mass density remain constant, the new fundamental frequency becomes $f_1' = \frac{1}{2L_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \frac{1}{2(5L_1/4)}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \frac{4}{5} \times 50 = 40$ Hz.

The second harmonic frequency is always twice the fundamental frequency. Initially $f_{2,\text{initial}} = 2 \times 50 = 100$ Hz, and after the change $f_{2,\text{final}} = 2 \times 40 = 80$ Hz.

The percentage change in the second harmonic frequency is $\frac{80 - 100}{100} \times 100\% = -20\%$, indicating a 20% decrease.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When source of sound and observer both are moving towards each other, the observer will hear
questions.solution:
When a source and observer move toward each other, the relative velocity increases, altering both frequency and wavelength through the Doppler effect.

The apparent frequency is given by $f' = f_0 \left( \frac{v + v_o}{v - v_s} \right), where $ v$ is the speed of sound, $v_o$ is the observer's speed, and $v_s$ is the source's speed. The positive terms $v_o$ and $v_s$ ensure \frac{v + v_o}{v - v_s} >1$, so $f' > f_0$.

Since $v = f\lambda$ remains constant, the wavelength must decrease as frequency increases: \lambda' = $\frac{v}{f'}$ < \lambda.$

The observer thus hears a high frequency and low wavelength, corresponding to option C.

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The lengths of the two organ pipes open at both ends are 'L' and $\left(L+L_1\right)$. If they are sounded together, the beat frequency will be ( $\mathrm{v}=$ velocity of sound in air)
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency for an organ pipe open at both ends is

$f = \frac{v}{2L}$

where

$L_1' = L$

and

$L_2' = L + L_1$

for the two pipes.

The frequencies are

$f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}$

and

$f_2 = \frac{v}{2(L + L_1)}$

giving a beat frequency of

$f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$

Substituting the expressions yields

$f_{\text{beat}} = \left| \frac{v}{2L} - \frac{v}{2(L + L_1)} \right| = \frac{v}{2} \left| \frac{1}{L} - \frac{1}{L + L_1} \right|$

Combining fractions inside the absolute value gives

$f_{\text{beat}} = \frac{v}{2} \left| \frac{(L + L_1) - L}{L(L + L_1)} \right| = \frac{v}{2} \cdot \frac{L_1}{L(L + L_1)}$

since

$L_1 > 0$

The expression

$\frac{v L_1}{2L(L + L_1)}$

corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person standing between two parallel cliffs fires a gun and hears two echoes, first echo after 1 second and the second echo after 3 second. The distance between the two cliffs is (Velocity of sound $=340 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ )
questions.solution:
Distance between cliffs using echo timing

Given sound velocity $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$, first echo time $t_1 = 1 \text{ s}$, and second echo time $t_2 = 3 \text{ s}$.

Since each echo corresponds to sound traveling to a cliff and back, the distance to the first cliff is $d_1 = v t_1 / 2 = 340 \text{ m/s} \times 1 \text{ s} / 2 = 170 \text{ m}$.

Similarly, distance to the second cliff is $d_2 = v t_2 / 2 = 340 \text{ m/s} \times 3 \text{ s} / 2 = 510 \text{ m}$.

The total distance between cliffs is $d_1 + d_2 = 170 \text{ m} + 510 \text{ m} = 680 \text{ m}$.

Therefore, the distance is $680 \text{ m}$ (Option B).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An organ pipe has fundamental frequency 80 Hz. If its one end is closed, the frequencies produced will be (in Hz ) (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
An organ pipe of length $L$ with fundamental frequency $80\text{ Hz}$ is initially open, satisfying $\frac{v}{2L} = 80$, where $v$ is the speed of sound.

When one end is closed, it becomes a closed pipe with fundamental frequency $f_{closed} = \frac{v}{4L} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 80 = 40\text{ Hz}$.

Closed pipes produce only odd harmonics: $f_{closed}, 3f_{closed}, 5f_{closed}, 7f_{closed}, \ldots$

Substituting $40\text{ Hz}$ yields the sequence $40, 120, 200, 280, \ldots\text{ Hz}$, which corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equation of wave is $y=60 \sin (1200 t-6 x)$, where ' $y$ ' is in micron, ' t ' is in second and ' x ' is in metre. The ratio of maximum particle velocity to the wave velocity of wave propagation is
questions.solution:
The wave equation $y = 60 \sin(1200t - 6x)$ has amplitude $A = 60 \times 10^{-6}$ m, angular frequency $\omega = 1200$ rad/s, and wave number $k = 6$ rad/m.

Maximum particle velocity is $v_{p,\text\max} = A\omega = (60 \times 10^{-6})(1200) = 0.072$ m/s.

Wave velocity is $v_w = \omega / k = 1200 / 6 = 200$ m/s.

The ratio $v_{p,\text\max} / v_w = A\omega / (\omega / k) = Ak = (60 \times 10^{-6})(6) = 3.6 \times 10^{-4}$, matching option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two waves of same frequency (n) are approaching each other with same velocity of $12 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ along the same linear path and interfere. The distance between two consecutive nodes is
questions.solution:
Standing waves form when two waves of identical frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions, with nodes being points of zero displacement.

The wave relationship $v = n\lambda$ connects velocity, frequency, and wavelength. Given $v = 12$ m/s, the wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{12}{n}$ m.

For standing waves, consecutive nodes are separated by half the wavelength, so the distance is $\frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{12}{n} = \frac{6}{n}$ m.

The correct choice is $\frac{6}{n}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two strings ' X ' and ' Y ' of a guitar produces a beat frequency of 6 Hz. When the tension of the string ' $Y$ ' is increased, the beat frequency is found to be 4 Hz. If the frequency of string ' X ' is 300 Hz , then the original frequency of string ' $Y$ ' is
questions.solution:
Given $f_X = 300\text{ Hz}$ produces a beat frequency of $6\text{ Hz}$ with string Y, the original frequency $f_Y$ satisfies $|300 - f_Y| = 6$. This yields possible values $f_Y = 294\text{ Hz}$ or $f_Y = 306\text{ Hz}$.

Increasing tension raises the frequency of string Y. With the new beat frequency reduced to $4\text{ Hz}$, the updated frequency $f_Y'$ satisfies $|300 - f_Y'| = 4$, giving possible values $f_Y' = 296\text{ Hz}$ or $f_Y' = 304\text{ Hz}$.

Since $f_Y' > f_Y$ under increased tension, the case $f_Y = 306\text{ Hz}$ is invalid—neither $296\text{ Hz}$ nor $304\text{ Hz}$ exceeds $306\text{ Hz}$. Only $f_Y = 294\text{ Hz}$ is consistent, as both possible new frequencies exceed $294\text{ Hz}$ and satisfy the beat condition.

The original frequency is therefore $\boxed{294\text{ Hz}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A transverse displacement of vibrating string is $y=0.06 \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right) x \cos (120 \pi t)$.
If the mass per unit length of a string is $4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{ kg} / \mathrm{m}$, then the tension in the string will be
questions.solution:
Given the transverse displacement $y = 0.06 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}x\right) \cos(120\pi t)$, comparison with the standard standing wave form $y = A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)$ identifies the wave number $k = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ rad/m and angular frequency $\omega = 120\pi$ rad/s.

The wave speed follows from $v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{120\pi}{\frac{2\pi}{3}} = 180$ m/s.

For a string with mass per unit length $\mu = 4 \times 10^{-2}$ kg/m, the speed of transverse waves obeys $v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$. Solving for tension yields $T = v^2 \mu = (180)^2 (4 \times 10^{-2}) = 1296$ N.

The tension in the string is 1296 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equation of a progressive wave is $Y=3 \sin \left[\pi \left(\frac{t}{3}-\frac{x}{5}\right)+\frac{\pi}{4}\right] where $x and y$ are in meter and time in second. Which of the following is correct?$
questions.solution:
The wave equation is given as $Y = 3 \sin \left[\pi \left(\frac{t}{3} - \frac{x}{5}\right) + \frac{\pi}{4}\right], which simplifies$ to Y = 3 \sin$\left(\frac{\pi t}{3} - \frac{\pi x}{5} + \frac{\pi}{4}\right).

Comparing$ with the standard formY = A \sin(\omegat - kx + \phi)$, the amplitude is A = 3$ m, angular frequency $\omega = \frac{\pi}{3}$rad/s, and wave number $k = \frac{\pi}{5}$rad/m.

The wavelength is given by $\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi/5} =10$ m, matching option A.

The wave velocity is $v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{\pi/3}{\pi/5} = \frac{5}{3} \approx1.67$ m/s, not $1.5$ m/s as in option B.

The frequency is $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{6} \approx0.167$ Hz, not $0.2$ Hz as in option D.

The correct choice is A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A vehicle starts from rest and accelerates along straight path at $2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. At the starting point of the vehicle, there is a stationary electric siren. How far has the vehicle nearly gone when the driver hears the siren at $94 \%$ of its value when the vehicle was at rest?
(speed of sound $=330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ )
questions.solution:
The vehicle's speed when the driver hears the siren at 94% of its original frequency is determined from the Doppler effect for a moving observer receding from a stationary source: $f' = f \left( \frac{v_s - v_o}{v_s} \right).

Given $ f' = 0.94f$ and $v_s = 330\,$\text{m/s}, solve for $ v_o$:

0.94 = \frac{330 - v_o}{330}
$ v_o = 330 - 0.94 $\times330 = 19.8\,\text{m/s}

With constant acceleration $ a = 2\,$\text{m/s}^2$ from rest, the distance traveled to reach this velocity is found from $v^2 = u² + 2ax$:

$19.8^2 = 0 + 2 $\cdot$2 $\cdot$ x$
$392.04 = 4x$
$x = 98.01\,\text{m}

Rounding to the nearest meter gives 98\,\text{m}$, corresponding to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pipe open at both ends of length 1.5 m is dipped in water at one end such that $2^{\text{nd }}$ overtone of vibrating air column is resonating with a tuning fork of frequency 330 Hz. The length of the pipe immersed in water is (Speed of sound in air $=330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}  ) (Neglect end correction)$
questions.solution:
A pipe open at both ends and partly immersed in water functions as a closed organ pipe.

The resonant frequencies of a closed pipe are $f_n = \frac{(2n-1)v}{4l}$, where $n$ is the harmonic number, $v$ is the speed of sound, and $l$ is the length of the air column.

The second overtone corresponds to the third harmonic ($n=3$).

Given $f = 330\,\text{Hz}$ and $v = 330\,\text{m/s}$, for resonance with the second overtone:

$330 = \frac{5 \times 330}{4l}$

Simplifying, $1 = \frac{5}{4l}$, so $l = \frac{5}{4} = 1.25\,\text{m}$.

The total pipe length is $1.5\,\text{m}$, so the immersed length is $1.5 - 1.25 = 0.25\,\text{m}$.

This corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two uniform wires of same material are vibrating under the same tension. If the $1^{\text{st }}$ overtone of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire is equal to the $2^{\text{nd }}$ overtone of $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire and radius of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire is twice the radius of $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire, the ratio of length of $1^{\text{st }}$ wire to that $2^{\text{nd }}$ wire is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency relationship for a string fixed at both ends gives the $n$th overtone frequency as $f_n = (n+1)\frac{v}{2L}$, where $v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ is the wave speed and $\mu = \rho\pi r^2$ is the mass per unit length for a wire of radius $r$ and density $\rho$.

Substituting yields $f_n = \frac{(n+1)}{2Lr}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$. For the first wire's first overtone ($n=1$), $f_1 = \frac{1}{L_1r_1}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$, and for the second wire's second overtone ($n=2$), $f_2 = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$.

Setting $f_1 = f_2$ and canceling the common factor $\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho\pi}}$ gives $\frac{1}{L_1r_1} = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}$. Given $r_1 = 2r_2$, substitution yields $\frac{1}{2L_1r_2} = \frac{3}{2L_2r_2}$, which simplifies to $\frac{1}{L_1} = \frac{3}{L_2}$.

The ratio is therefore $L_1:L_2 = 1:3$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An observer on sea-coast counts 45 waves in one minute. If the wavelength of the waves is 7 m , then the velocity of the waves will be
questions.solution:
Wave velocity is determined using the fundamental relationship $v = f \lambda$, where $f$ is frequency and $\lambda$ is wavelength.

Frequency is computed as waves per second. Given 45 waves in 60 seconds:

$f = \frac{45}{60} = 0.75$ Hz

Substituting $f = 0.75$ Hz and $\lambda = 7$ m:

$v = 0.75 \times 7 = 5.25$ m/s

The calculated velocity of 5.25 m/s corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two sources of sound are emitting progressive waves $y_1=4 \sin 710 \pi t$ and $y_2=3 \sin 702 \pi t$. The sources are placed close to each other. The number of beats heard per second and intensity ratio between waxing and waning are respectively
questions.solution: The progressive waves are given as $y_1 = 4 \sin 710 \pi t$ and $y_2 = 3 \sin 702 \pi t$. From the standard wave form $y = A \sin \omega t$, the amplitudes are $A_1 = 4$ and $A_2 = 3$, with angular frequencies $\omega_1 = 710 \pi$ rad/s and $\omega_2 = 702 \pi$ rad/s. The beat frequency is the difference in the individual frequencies. Since $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}$, $f_1 = 355$ Hz and $f_2 = 351$ Hz, so $f_{\text{beat}} = |355 - 351| = 4$ beats/s. Under constructive and destructive interference, the maximum and minimum amplitudes are $A_{\text\max} = A_1 + A_2 = 7$ and $A_{\text\min} = |A_1 - A_2| = 1$. Since intensity $I \propto A^2$, the ratio is $\frac{I_{\text\max}{I_{\text\min}}} = \frac{7^2}{1^2} = \frac{49}{1}$. The number of beats per second is 4 and the intensity ratio is 49:1, so the correct option is C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $The closed and open organ pipe have same length and when they are vibrating simultaneously in first overtone produce 3 beats. The length of open pipe is made \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\mathrm{rd}}$ and that of closed pipe is made 3 times the original, the number of beats produced will be (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Beat frequency analysis for organ pipes with length modifications

Let $v$ represent the speed of sound in air and $L$ the original length of both pipes.

The first overtone for an open pipe is $f_{o1} = v/L$, while for a closed pipe it is $f_{c1} = 3v/4L$.

The initial beat frequency of 3 Hz gives $|v/L - 3v/4L| = 3$, simplifying to $v/(4L) = 3$ and thus $v/L = 12$.

After modification, the open pipe length becomes $L/3$ and the closed pipe length becomes $3L$.

The fundamental frequencies are now $f'_{o} = v/(2 \cdot L/3) = 3v/(2L)$ for the open pipe and $f'_{c} = v/(4 \cdot 3L) = v/(12L)$ for the closed pipe.

The beat frequency becomes $|3v/(2L) - v/(12L)| = |18v/(12L) - v/(12L)| = 17v/(12L)$.

Substituting $v/L = 12$ yields $17 \cdot 12 / 12 = 17$ Hz.

Final answer: $\boxed{17}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The length of closed and open pipe is same. The ratio of frequency of $\mathrm{n}^{\text{th }}$ overtone for closed pipe to that of open pipe is (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
The frequency of the $n$th overtone for a closed pipe is $f_{c,n} = (2n+1) \frac{v}{4L}$, while for an open pipe it is $f_{o,n} = (n+1) \frac{v}{2L}$.

The ratio is then

$\frac{f_{c,n}}{f_{o,n}} = \frac{(2n+1) \frac{v}{4L}}{(n+1) \frac{v}{2L}} = \frac{(2n+1)}{2(n+1)}$.

The correct answer is A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The apparent wavelength of light from a star moving away from the earth is $0.02 \%$ more than the actual wavelength. The velocity of star is $\left[\mathrm{c}=\right.velocity of $light $\left.=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right]$
questions.solution:
Doppler effect analysis: The apparent wavelength is $0.02\%$ greater than the actual wavelength, giving $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = 0.0002$.

For a receding light source, the relativistic Doppler shift formula simplifies to $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{c}$ when $v \ll c$.

Substituting values: $\frac{v}{c} = 0.0002$

$v = 0.0002 \times 3 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{m/s} = 6 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{m/s}$

Converting to kilometers per second: $v = 60\ \mathrm{km/s}$

This result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The frequency of a stretched uniform wire of length $L$ under tension is in resonance with the fundamental frequency of a closed pipe of same length. If the tension in the wire is increased by 8 N , it is in resonance with the first overtone of the same closed pipe. The initial tension in the wire is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is given by $f_{\text{wire}} = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{T / \mu}$, and that of a closed pipe is $f_{\text{pipe,0}} = v / (4L)$.

Initially, resonance occurs between the wire's fundamental and the pipe's fundamental: $\frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{T_1 / \mu} = v / (4L)$. Simplifying yields $\sqrt{T_1 / \mu} = v / 2$, so $T_1 = \mu v^2 / 4$.

After increasing tension by 8 N, $T_2 = T_1 + 8$, resonance occurs with the pipe's first overtone at $3v / (4L)$: $\frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{T_2 / \mu} = 3v / (4L)$. This simplifies to $\sqrt{T_2 / \mu} = 3v / 2$, giving $T_2 = 9 \mu v^2 / 4$.

Dividing the expressions for $T_2$ and $T_1$ results in $T_2 / T_1 = 9$. Substituting $T_2 = T_1 + 8$ leads to $(T_1 + 8) / T_1 = 9$, hence $T_1 + 8 = 9T_1$, $8 = 8T_1$, and $T_1 = 1$ N.

The initial tension is 1 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When an observer moves towards a stationary source with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_1$ ', the appearent frequency of emitted note is ' $\mathrm{F}_1$ '. When observer moves away from stationary source with velocity ' $\mathrm{V}_1$ ' the appearent frequency is ' $F_2$ '. If ' $v$ ' is velocity of sound in air and $\frac{F_1}{F_2}=2$, then $\frac{V}{V_1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The Doppler effect for sound waves gives the apparent frequency $F'$ when an observer moves relative to a stationary source:

$F' = F \left( \frac{v \pm V_o}{v} \right)

where $ F$ is the source frequency, $v$ the speed of sound, and $V_o$ the observer's speed.

When the observer approaches the source, the apparent frequency is $F_1 = F $\left( \frac{v + V_1}{v} \right)$.

When moving away, $F_2 = F \left( \frac{v - V_1}{v} \right).

Given \frac{F_1}{F_2} =2$, substitute the expressions:

$\frac{v + V_1}{v - V_1} =2$

Solving for $\frac{v}{V_1}:

$2(v - V_1) = v + V_1$
$2v - 2V_1 = v + V_1$
$v = 3V_1$

Thus \frac{v}{V_1} =$3$, corresponding to option C.

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In fundamental mode, the time required for the sound wave to reach up to closed end of a pipe filled with air is 't' second. The frequency of vibration of air column is (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency of a closed pipe

For a pipe closed at one end vibrating in its fundamental mode, the pipe length equals one quarter of the wavelength: $L = \frac{\lambda}{4}$.

The speed of sound relates to frequency and wavelength by $v = f\lambda$.

The sound wave travels the pipe length $L$ in time $t$, giving $L = vt$.

Combining these relationships yields $\lambda = 4L = 4vt$. Substituting into the wave equation: $v = f(4vt)$.

Solving for frequency: $f = \frac{1}{4t} = (4t)^{-1}$.

The expression matches option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two pipes of lengths $\mathrm{L}_1$ and $\mathrm{L}_2$, open at both ends are joined in series. If ' $f_1$ ' and ' $f_2$ ' are the fundamental frequencies of two pipes, then the fundamental frequency of series combination will be (neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency for an open pipe is given by $f = \frac{v}{2L}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound and $L$ is the pipe length.

The individual pipe lengths are $L_1 = \frac{v}{2f_1}$ and $L_2 = \frac{v}{2f_2}$.

When joined in series, the total length becomes $L_{\text{total}} = L_1 + L_2 = \frac{v}{2}\left(\frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}\right) = \frac{v}{2} \cdot \frac{f_1 + f_2}{f_1 f_2}$.

The fundamental frequency of the combined pipe is then:

$f_{\text{total}} = \frac{v}{2L_{\text{total}}} = \frac{v}{2 \cdot \frac{v}{2} \cdot \frac{f_1 + f_2}{f_1 f_2}} = \frac{1}{\frac{f_1 + f_2}{f_1 f_2}} = \frac{f_1 f_2}{f_1 + f_2}$.

The result corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $L$, diameter ' $d$ ' density of material ' $Q$ ' is under tension ' T ', having fundamental frequency of vibration $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}$. Another wire of length 2 L , tension 2 T , density 2 Q and diameter 3 d has fundamental frequency of vibration $n_B$. The ratio $n_B: n_A$ is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of vibration for a stretched wire is given by $n = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, where $L$ is length, $T$ is tension, and $\mu$ is linear mass density.

The linear mass density relates to material density $\rho$ and cross-sectional area as $\mu = \rho A = \rho \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$, where $d$ is the wire diameter.

Substituting gives $n = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho \pi d^2 / 4}} = \frac{1}{Ld} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho \pi}}$.

For wire A with $L_A = L$, $d_A = d$, $\rho_A = Q$, and $T_A = T$:
$n_A = \frac{1}{Ld} \sqrt{\frac{T}{Q \pi}}$.

For wire B with $L_B = 2L$, $d_B = 3d$, $\rho_B = 2Q$, and $T_B = 2T$:
$n_B = \frac{1}{(2L)(3d)} \sqrt{\frac{2T}{(2Q) \pi}} = \frac{1}{6Ld} \sqrt{\frac{T}{Q \pi}}$.

The ratio is $\frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $n_B : n_A = 1:6$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The frequency of a tuning fork is 256 Hz. It will <u>not</u> resonate with the tuning fork of frequency
questions.solution:
Resonance occurs when frequencies are exact integer multiples. Given $f_0 = 256\text{ Hz}$, the harmonic frequencies are $n \times 256\text{ Hz}$ for integer $n$.

The frequency $754\text{ Hz}$ is approximately $2.945f_0$, which is not an integer multiple of $256\text{ Hz}$ and will not resonate.$512\text{ Hz} = 2f_0$ and $768\text{ Hz} = 3f_0$ are harmonics and will resonate.

The tuning fork that does not resonate is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an organ pipe closed at one end, the sum of the frequencies of first three overtones is 3930 Hz. The frequency of the fundamental mode of organ pipe is
questions.solution:
For an organ pipe closed at one end, the harmonic frequencies are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency $f_1$. The first three overtones correspond to the third, fifth, and seventh harmonics, with frequencies $3f_1$, $5f_1$, and $7f_1$, respectively.

The sum of these overtone frequencies is given as 3930 Hz:

$3f_1 + 5f_1 + 7f_1 = 3930$

which simplifies to

$15f_1 = 3930$

Solving for $f_1$:

$f_1 = \frac{3930}{15} = 262$ Hz

The fundamental frequency is 262 Hz, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A progressive wave of frequency 400 Hz is travelling with velocity $336 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. How far apart are the two points on a wave which are $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ out of phase?
questions.solution:
The wavelength is determined from the wave velocity and frequency using $v = f\lambda$.

Given $f = 400\,\text{Hz}$ and $v = 336\,\text{m/s}$, the wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{336}{400} = 0.84\,\text{m}$.

The phase difference $\Delta\phi$ and path difference $\Delta x$ are related by $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$.

A phase difference of $60^{}^{\circ}$ corresponds to $\Delta\phi = \frac{\pi}{3}\,\text{rad}$.

Solving for the path difference yields $\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\Delta\phi = \frac{0.84}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{0.84}{6} = 0.14\,\text{m}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{0.14\,\text{m}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When two tuning forks are sounded together, 6 beats per second are heard. One of the fork is in unison with 0.70 m length of sonometer wire and another fork is in unison with 0.69 m length of the same sonometer wire. The frequencies of the two tuning forks are
questions.solution:
When two tuning forks produce 6 beats per second, the difference in their frequencies is 6 Hz: $|f_1 - f_2| = 6$.

The frequency of a vibrating sonometer wire is inversely proportional to its length, $f \propto 1/L$, so $fL$ remains constant for constant tension and linear density. Given $L_1 = 0.70 \text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.69 \text{ m}$, the frequencies satisfy $f_1 L_1 = f_2 L_2$.

Since $L_1 > L_2$, it follows that $f_1 < f_2$, so the beat frequency equation becomes $f_2 - f_1 = 6$.

Substitute $f_1 = f_2 L_2 / L_1$ into the beat equation: $f_2 - (0.69 / 0.70) f_2 = 6$. Simplify to $f_2 (1 - 0.69 / 0.70) = 6$, yielding $f_2 (0.01 / 0.70) = 6$. Solve for $f_2 = 6 \times 0.70 / 0.01 = 420 \text{ Hz}$.

Then $f_1 = 420 - 6 = 414 \text{ Hz}$.

The frequencies are $414 \text{ Hz}$ and $420 \text{ Hz}$, corresponding to option B.

The answer is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When source of sound moves towards a stationary observer, the apparent frequency heard by him
options: remains the same while wavelength decreases.
decreases and wavelength remains the same.
questions.solution:
For a sound source moving toward a stationary observer, the Doppler effect causes both frequency and wavelength to change.

The apparent frequency is given by $f' = f \left( \frac{v}{v - v_s} \right), where $ v$ is the speed of sound, $f$ is the source frequency, and $v_s$ is the source speed. Since $v_s > 0$, the denominator $v - v_s < v$, making $f' > f$. The frequency increases.

The apparent wavelength becomes \lambda' = \frac{v - v_s}{f}. Comparing to the original wavelength \lambda = \frac{v}{f}, we have \lambda' = \lambda - \frac{v_s}{f}, which is less than \lambda$ since $v_s > 0$. The wavelength decreases.

Therefore, both frequency increases and wavelength decrease, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The frequency of fourth overtone of a closed pipe is in unison with the fifth overtone of an open pipe. The ratio of length of closed pipe to that of open pipe is
questions.solution:
The fourth overtone of a closed pipe is in unison with the fifth overtone of an open pipe, so their frequencies are equal.

For a closed pipe, the $n^{\text{th}}$ overtone has frequency $f_c = (2n+1)\frac{v}{4L_c}$. Setting $n=4$ gives $f_{c} = 9\frac{v}{4L_c}$.

For an open pipe, the $n^{\text{th}}$ overtone has frequency $f_o = (n+1)\frac{v}{2L_o}$. With $n=5$, $f_o = 6\frac{v}{2L_o}$.

Equating the frequencies yields:

$9\frac{v}{4L_c} = 6\frac{v}{2L_o}$

Cancel $v$ and simplify:

$\frac{9}{4L_c} = \frac{3}{L_o}$

Rearranging gives $\frac{L_c}{L_o} = \frac{9}{4} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3}{4}$.

The ratio of lengths is $L_c : L_o = 3 : 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string of mass $0.1 \mathrm{kgm}^{-1}$ has length 0.9 m. It is fixed at both ends and stretched such that it has a tension of 40 N. The string vibrates in three segments with amplitude 0.3 cm. The amplitude (maximum) of the particle velocity is (in m/s)
questions.solution:
Maximum particle velocity amplitude is determined from the angular frequency and vibration amplitude: $u_{\text\max} = A \omega$.

The wave speed is $v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{40}{0.1}} = 20$ m/s.

For the third harmonic on a fixed string, wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{2L}{n} = \frac{2 \times 0.9}{3} = 0.6$ m.

Frequency becomes $f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{20}{0.6} = \frac{100}{3}$ Hz, yielding angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f = \frac{200\pi}{3}$ rad/s.

Given vibration amplitude $A = 0.3 \times 10^{-2}$ m, then $u_{\text\max} = A \omega = \left(0.3 \times 10^{-2}\right) \cdot \frac{200\pi}{3} = \frac{60\pi}{300} = \frac{\pi}{5}$ m/s.

This corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of a closed pipe of length $L$ is equal to the second overtone of a pipe open at both the ends of length (XL). The value of X is (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
th $L' = XL$ yields:

$\frac{v}{4L} = \frac{3v}{2XL}$

Canceling $v$ and $L$ from both sides gives $\frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{2X}$.

Solving for $X$ produces $2X = 12$, so $X = 6$.

The value of $X$ is 6, corresponding to option $\boxed{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two sound waves having frequencies 250 Hz and 256 Hz superimpose to produce beat wave. The resultant beat wave has intensity maximum at $t=0$. After how much time an intensity will be minimum produced at the same point?
questions.solution:
Beat frequency $=256-250=6 \mathrm{ Hz}$
Time between the maxima and minima of the beats is $\frac{T_{\text{beats }}}{2}$.
$\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\text{beats }}}{2}=\frac{1}{6 \times 2}=\frac{1}{12} \mathrm{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A pipe 60 cm long and open at both the ends produces harmonics. Which harmonic mode of pipe resonates a 2.2 KHz source?
(Speed of sound in air $=330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s})$ (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Here, $l=60 \mathrm{ cm}, v=2200 \mathrm{ Hz}, \dot{\mathrm{v}}=330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. If $\mathrmn^{\text{th }}$ harmonic of pipe resonates with the source, then for a open pipe,
$\begin{aligned}
v & =\mathrm{n} \frac{\mathrm{v}}{2 l_{\mathrm{o}}} \\
2200 & =\mathrm{n}\left[\frac{330}{2 \times\left(60 \times 10^{-2}\right)}\right] \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{n} & =\frac{2 \times\left(60 \times 10^{-2}\right) \times 2200}{330}=8
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source and listener are both moving towards each other with speed $\frac{\mathrm{V}}{10}$. (where V is speed of sound) If the frequency of sound note emitted by the source is ' $n$ ', then the frequency heard by the listener would be nearly
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrmn^{\prime} & =\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}+\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mathrm{V}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}}}\right) \mathrm{n} \\ & =\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}+\frac{\mathrm{V}}{10}}{\mathrm{ V}-\frac{\mathrm{V}}{10}}\right) \mathrm{n} \\ & =\frac{11}{9} \mathrm{n} \\ & =1.22 \mathrm{n}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two uniform strings A and B made of steel are made to vibrate under the same tension. If first overtone of A is equal to the second overtone of B and if the radius of A is twice that of B , the ratio of the length of string $B$ to that of $A$ is
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{R}_2=2 \mathrm{R}_1, \mathrm{ T}_1=\mathrm{T}_2$
As the first overtone of A is equal to second overtone of B, we get $\begin{aligned} 2 n_A=3 n_B \\ \ldots(\because \text{ first overtone }=\text{ second } \end{aligned}$ harmonic)...(i) Also, $\mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}}{\mathrm{ m}}}$. Where, $\mathrm{m}=$ mass per unit length $=\frac{\left(\pi \mathrm{R}^2 l\right) \rho}{l} . .(\mathrm{ii})\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad 2 \times \frac{1}{2 l_{\mathrm{A}}} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}}{\mathrm{ m}_{\mathrm{A}}}}=3 \times \frac{1}{2 l_B} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}}{\mathrm{ m}_{\mathrm{B}}}} ...(from(i))\\ & \therefore \quad \frac{l_{\mathrm{A}}}{l_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ m}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{ m}_{\mathrm{A}}}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\pi \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}^2}{\pi \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}^2}} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{l_{\mathrm{A}}}{l_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}^2}{\left(2 \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}}\right)^2}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{3} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{l_{\mathrm{B}}}{l_{\mathrm{A}}}=\frac{3}{1} \end{aligned}$ ...(from (ii))

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string is under tension of 180 N and mass per unit length $2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Kg} / \mathrm{m}$. It produces two consecutive resonant frequencies with a tuning fork, which are 375 Hz and 450 Hz. The mass of the string is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \text{ Fundamental frequency } & =\mathrm{f}_2-\mathrm{f}_1 \\ & =450-375 \\ & =75 \mathrm{ Hz}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{f} & =\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{ L}} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}}{\mu}} \\
75 & =\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{ L}} \sqrt{\frac{180}{2 \times 10^{-3}}} \\
\mathrm{ L} & =2 \mathrm{ m} \\
\mu & =\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{ L}} \\

& =4 \text{ gram }

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: How many times more intense is a 60 dB sound than a 30 dB sound?
questions.solution:
Loudness of two sounds are given as $\mathrm{L}_2=60 \mathrm{ dB}$ and $\mathrm{L}_1=30 \mathrm{ dB}$
Loudness of sound $L=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}_0}\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \quad & L_2-L_1=10 \log _{10} \frac{I_2}{I_1} \\
& 60-30=10 \log _{10} \frac{I_2}{I_1} \\
\therefore \quad & \log _{10} \frac{I_2}{I_1}=3 \\
& \frac{I_2}{I_1}=10^3 \Rightarrow I_2=1000 I_1
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two sound waves each of wavelength ' $\lambda$ ' and having the same amplitude ' A ' from two source ' $\mathrm{S}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{S}_2$ ' interfere at a point P. If the path difference, $\mathrm{S}_2 \mathrm{P}-\mathrm{S}_1 \mathrm{P}=\lambda / 3$ then the amplitude of resultant wave at point ' P ' will be $\left[\cos   \left(120^{{}^{\circ}}\right)=$-0.5\right]
questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \text{ Path difference }=\frac{\lambda}{3} \\ \therefore \quad & \text{ Phase difference }=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}=120^{{}^{\circ}} \\ & \text{ Resultant amplitude } \\ & \mathrm{R}=\sqrt{\mathrm{A}_1^2+\mathrm{A}_2^2+2 \mathrm{ A}_1 \mathrm{ A}_2 \cos \theta} \\ \therefore \quad & \text{ Since, } \mathrm{A}_1=\mathrm{A}_2 \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{R}=\sqrt{\mathrm{A}^2+\mathrm{A}^2+2 \mathrm{ A}^2 \cos 120^{{}^{\circ}}} \\ \quad & \mathrm{R}=\sqrt{\mathrm{A}^2+\mathrm{A}^2+2 \mathrm{ A}^2 \times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{A}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An open organ pipe of length ' $l$ ' is sounded together with another open organ pipe of length $\left(l+l_1\right)$ in their fundamental modes. Speed of sound in air is ' $V$ '. The beat frequency heard will be ( $l_1 \ll l$ )
questions.solution:
For a pipe open at both ends, $\mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 l}\therefore \quad \mathrm{f}_1=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 l} \quad ; \quad \mathrm{f}_2=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2\left(l+l_1\right)}\therefore \quad$ beat frequency, $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{b}}=\mathrm{f}_1-\mathrm{f}_2=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 l}-\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2\left(l+l_1\right)}\therefore \quad \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{b}}=\mathrm{V}\left[\frac{2\left(l+l_1\right)-2 l}{4 l\left(l+l_1\right)}\right]=\mathrm{V} \frac{2 l_1}{4 l\left(l+l_1\right)}\therefore \quad \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{V} l_1}{2 l\left(l+l_1\right)}$
Since $l_1 \ll l, l_1$ in the denominator can be taken as zero.
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{V} l_1}{2 l^2}$

questions.q: Two progressive waves $Y_1=\sin 2 \pi \left(\frac{t}{0 \cdot 4}-\frac{x}{4}\right)$ and  $\mathrm{Y}_{2}=\sin 2 \pi  \left(\frac{\mathrm{t}}{0 \cdot 4}+\frac{\mathrm{x}}{4}\right)superpose to form a standing wave. ' $ x$ ' and ' $y$ ' are in SI system. Amplitude of the particle at $x=0.5  $\mathrm{ m}is \left[\sin45^{{}^{\circ}}=\cos 45^{{}^{\circ}}=\f frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right]$
questions.solution: $Y=Y_1+Y_2\begin{array}{ll}\therefore \quad & Y=\sin\left(\frac{2 \pi t}{0.4}-\frac{2 \pi x}{4}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{2 \pi t}{0.4}+\frac{2 \pi x}{4}\right) \\ & \sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)=2 \sin A \cos B \\ \therefore \quad & Y=2 \sin\left(\frac{2 \pi t}{0.4}\right), \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi x}{4}\right) \\ & Y=R \sin\left(\frac{2 \pi t}{0.4}\right), \text{ where } R \text{ is the amplitude } \\ \therefore \quad & R=2 \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi x}{4}\right) \\ \therefore \quad & \text{ at } x=0.5 \\ & R=2 \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{4 \times 2}\right)=2 \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the velocity of sound in hydrogen gas $\left(\gamma=\frac{7}{5}\right)$ to that in helium gas $\left(\gamma=\frac{5}{3}\right)$ at the same temperature is
questions.solution:
Formula: $\frac{v_H}{v_{H e}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_H M_{H e}}{\gamma_{H e} M_H}} .$
Given: - $\gamma_H=\frac{7}{5}, \gamma_{H e}=\frac{5}{3}$, - $M_H=2, M_{H e}=4$.
Substitute values: $\frac{v_H}{v_{H e}}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{7}{5} \cdot 4}{\frac{5}{3} \cdot 2}}=\sqrt{\frac{28}{10} \cdot \frac{3}{5}}=\sqrt{\frac{84}{50}}=\frac{\sqrt{42}}{5} .$
Answer: $\frac{\sqrt{42}}{5}$, Option 4.

It is observed that wire resonates in the $\mathrmP^{\mathrm{th}}$ harmonic at a frequency of 320 Hz and resonates again at next higher frequency of 400 Hz. The value of ' $p$ ' is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & 320=\frac{\mathrm{p}}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ F}}{\mu}} \text{$ and $} 400=\frac{\mathrm{p}+1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ F}}{\mu}} \\ & \frac{400}{320}=\frac{\mathrm{p}+1}{\mathrm{p}} \Rightarrow 400 \mathrm{p}=320 \mathrm{p}+320 \\ & \mathrm{p}=4\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The frequency of two tuning forks A and B are respectively $1.4 \%$ more and $2.6 \%$ less than that of the tuning fork C. When A and B are sounded together, 10 beats are produced in 1 second. The frequency of tuning fork C is
questions.solution:
Let n be the frequency of fork C $\therefore \quad \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{n}+\frac{1.4 \mathrm{n}}{100}=\frac{101.4 \mathrm{n}}{100} \text{ and } \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{n}-\frac{2.6 \mathrm{n}}{100}=\frac{97.4 \mathrm{n}}{100}$
But $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}=10 \Rightarrow \frac{4 \mathrm{n}}{100}=10 \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=250 $$\mathrm{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resonance tube closed at one end is of height 1.5 m. A tuning fork of frequency 340 Hz is vibrating above the tube. Water is poured in the tube gradually. The minimum height of water column for which resonance is obtained is. (Neglect end correction, speed of sound in air $=340 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ )
questions.solution:
For a resonance tube, In the first mode, we have $\mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{4 \mathrm{ L}_{\mathrm{j}}}$ or $\mathrm{L}_1=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{4 \mathrm{n}}=\frac{340}{4 \times 340}=0.25 \mathrm{ m}=25 \mathrm{ cm}$
In this case $\mathrm{L}_1=\frac{\lambda}{4}=25 \mathrm{ cm} \Rightarrow \lambda=100 \mathrm{ cm}$
Resonance can also be obtained when the length of the air column is $\frac{3 \lambda}{4}, \frac{5 \lambda}{4}, \frac{7 \lambda}{4}$ etc.
At $\frac{5 \lambda}{4}=\frac{5 \times 100}{4}=125 \mathrm{ cm}$ it stops as length of tube is $1.5 \mathrm{ m}=150 \mathrm{ cm}$.
Hence the minimum height of water $=150-125=25 \mathrm{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At the poles of earth, a stretched wire of a given length vibrates in unison with a tuning fork. At the equator of earth, for same setting, to produce resonance with same fork, the vibrating length of wire
options: should be three times the original.
questions.solution:
For a string,
Frequency of vibration $n=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}}{\mathrm{ m}}}$
If $\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{Mg}$, then $\mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Mg}}{\mathrm{m}}}$
If $l_1$ and $g_1$ are the length and acceleration due to gravity at the poles and $l_2$ and $g_2$ at the equator respectively, then if the frequency is the same,
$\begin{array}{ll} & \mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{2 l_1} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Mg}_1}{\mathrm{ m}}}=\frac{1}{2 l_2} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Mg}_2}{\mathrm{ m}}} \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{ g}_1}}{l_1}=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{g}_2}}{l_2} \text{ or } \frac{l_2}{l_1}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{g}_2}{\mathrm{ g}_1}} \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{ g}_2 < \mathrm{g}_1 \\
\therefore \quad & l_2 < l_1
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With what velocity an observer should move relative to a stationary source so that a sound of triple the frequency of source is heard by an observer?
options: Same as velocity of sound towards the source.
Same as velocity of sound away from the source.
Half the velocity of sound towards the source.
Twice the velocity of sound towards the source.
questions.solution:
Applying Doppler's effect to sound waves, we can write, $n^{\prime}=n \left(\frac{v+v_0}{v}\right)=n \lleft(1+\frac{v_0}{v}\right).\begin{array}{ll} & \mathrm{n}^{\prime}=3 n \quad \ldots . \text{ (given) }\\
\therefore \quad & 3  n=n\l left(1+\frac{v_0}{v}\right)\\
\therefore \quad & 3=1+\frac{v_0}{v}\\
\therefore \quad & \frac{v_0}{v}=2 \quad \Rightarrow v_0=2 v
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The length of a sonometer wire ' AB ' is 110 cm. Where should the two bridges be placed from end ' A ' to divide the wire in three segments whose fundamental frequencies are in the ratio $1: 2: 3$ ?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{L}_1+\mathrm{L}_2+\mathrm{L}_3=110 \mathrm{ cm} \text{$ and $} \\
& \mathrm{n}_1 \mathrm{ L}_1=\mathrm{n}_2 \mathrm{ L}_2=\mathrm{n}_3 \mathrm{ L}_3 \\
& \text{ Required condition, } \mathrm{n}_1: \mathrm{n}_2: \mathrm{n}_3:: 1: 2: 3
\end{aligned}$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \quad & $\frac{n_1}{n_2}=\frac{1}{2}=\frac{L_2}{L_1}$ \Rightarrow L_2=$\frac{L_1}{2} \text{$ and } \\
& $\frac{n_1}{n_3}=\frac{1}{3}=\frac{L_3}{L_1}$ \Rightarrow L_3=$\frac{L_1}{3}$ \\
\therefore \quad & L_1+$\frac{L_1}{2}+\frac{L_1}{3}=$110 \\
\therefore \quad & L_1=60 $\mathrm{ cm}$ ; L_2=30 $\mathrm{ cm}$, L_3=20 $\mathrm{ cm}$
\end{array}$\therefore \quad$ The two bridges should be kept at 60 cm and 60+30=90 $\mathrm{ cm}$ .

questions.q: A sonometer wire is in unison with a tuning fork of frequency ' $n$ ' when it is stretched by a weight of specific gravity ' $d$ '. When the weight is completely immersed in water, ' $x$ ' beats are produced per second, then
questions.solution:
For Sonometer,
We know, relative density $\sigma=\frac{\rho_{\text{load }}}{\rho_{\text{water }}}$
Also, $\mathrm{n} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{T}}$
Tension in air $\mathrm{T}_{\text{air }}=\rho_{\text{load }} \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{g}$
Tension in water $\mathrm{T}_{\text{water }}=\left(\rho_{\text{load }}-\rho_{\text{water }}\right) \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{g}=\rho_{\text{water }} \cdot(\sigma-1) \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \dot{\mathrm{~g}}\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{load in air }}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{load inmersed in water }}}=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{T}_{\text{air }}}}{\sqrt{T_{\text{water }}}}$
On substituting the respective values,
$\frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{load in air }}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{load immersed in water }}}=\frac{\sqrt{\rho_{\text{load }} \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{g}}}{\sqrt{\rho_{\text{water }} \cdot(\sigma-1) \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\text{load }}}{\sigma_{\text{load }}-1}}...(i)$
where, $\sigma=$ relative density or specific gravity of load
Given, $\mathrm{n}_{\text{load }}=$ frequency
$\therefore \quad$ ' $x$ ' beats are produced when weight is completely immersed in water
$\mathrm{n}_{\text{load }}$ in water $=\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{x}$
Given, Specific gravity of load $\left(\sigma_{\text{load }}\right)=d\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{x}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{~d}-1}}$
...[From(i)]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tuning fork of frequency 340 Hz is vibrated just above a tube of 120 cm height. Water is slowly poured in the tube. What is the minimum height of water necessary for resonance?
questions.solution:
Because the tuning fork is in resonance with air column with a pipe closed at one end, the frequency is $\mathrm{n}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{ N}-1) \mathrm{v}}{4 l}$ where $\mathrm{N}=1,2,3 \ldots$. corresponds to different modes of vibration Substituting $\mathrm{n}=340 \mathrm{ Hz}, \mathrm{v}=340 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ (speed of sound in air), the length of air column in the pipe can be $l=\frac{(2 \mathrm{ N}-1) 340}{4 \times 340}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{ N}-1)}{4} \mathrm{ m}=\frac{(2 \mathrm{ N}-1) \times 100}{4} \mathrm{ cm}$
For $\mathrm{N}=1,2,3, \ldots$ we get $\cdot l=25 \mathrm{ cm}, 75 \mathrm{ cm}$, $125 \mathrm{ cm}..$. etc. As the tube is only 120 cm long, length of air column after water is poured in it may be 25 cm or 75 cm only. Hence, the corresponding length of water column in the tube will be $(120-25) \mathrm{cm}=95 \mathrm{ cm}$ or $(120-75) \mathrm{cm}=45 \mathrm{ cm}$. Thus minimum length of water column is 45 cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stationery wave is represented by $y=12 \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{6} x\right) \sin (8 \pi t)$, where $x \ \text{ and } y$ are in $c m$ and $t$ in second. The distance between two successive antinodes is
questions.solution:
Given equation for stationary wave,
$y=12 \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{6} x\right) \sin (8 \pi t)$Comparing this equation with standard stationary wave equation,
$y=2 A \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi x}{\lambda}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} t\right)\begin{aligned}
& \text{ We get, } \\
& \frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}=\frac{\pi}{6} \\
& \therefore \quad \lambda=12 \mathrm{ cm}
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Distance between two successive antinodes =$\frac{\lambda}{2}=$6 $\mathrm{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A transverse wave travelling along a stretched string has a speed of $30 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ and a frequency of 250 Hz. The phase difference between two points on the string 10 cm apart at the same instant is
questions.solution:
The wavelength of the wave is given by,
$\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{30}{250}=0.12 \mathrm{ m} Also,$ the phase difference '\phi$ ' is given by, $\phi=$\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}$ \times$ path difference
 \begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \phi=\frac{2 \pi(0.1)}{\lambda} \\
& \text{...(path difference }=\\
& 10 \mathrm{ cm}=0.1 \mathrm{ m} \text{ ) } \\
& \therefore \quad \phi=\frac{2 \pi}{0.12} \times 0.1 \\
& \therefore \quad \phi=\left(\frac{5 \pi}{3}\right)^{\text{radian}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train sounding a whistle of frequency 510 Hz approaches a station at $72 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{hr}$. The frequency of the note heard by an observer on the platform as the train (1) approaches the station and then (2) recedes the station are respectively (in hertz) (velocity of sound in air $=320 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ )
questions.solution:
Given, Frequency of source $\left(n_0\right)=510 \mathrm{~Hz}$ Velocity of source $=72 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{hr}=72 \times \frac{5}{18}=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
Velocity of sound in air $=320 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Doppler formula for apparent frequency, when source is approaching a stationary listener, $n_1=n_0\left(\frac{v}{v-v_s}\right)\therefore \quad \mathrm{n}_1=510 \times\left(\frac{320}{320-20}\right)=544 \mathrm{~Hz}$ Doppler formula for apparent frequency, when source is moving away from a stationary listener, $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_0\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}}\right) \\ & \mathrm{n}_2=510 \times\left(\frac{320}{320+20}\right)=480 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A set of 28 turning forks is arranged in an increasing order of frequencies. Each fork produces ' $x$ ' beats per second with the preceding fork and the last fork is an octave of the first. If the frequency of the $12^{\text{th }}$ fork is 152 Hz , the value of ' $x$ ' (no. of beats per second) is
questions.solution:
Forks arranged in a series of increasing frequency from $\mathrm{n}_1$ to $\mathrm{n}_{28}$ Each for produces ' $x$ ' beats with preceding fork, $\therefore \quad$ For. $12^{\text{th }}$ fork, $\mathrm{n}_{12}=\mathrm{n}_1+11 \mathrm{x}\therefore \quad 152=\mathrm{n}_1+11 \mathrm{x}$ Similarly, $\mathrm{n}_{28}=\mathrm{n}_1+27 \mathrm{x}$
Given condition is $\mathrm{n}_{28}=2 \mathrm{n}_12 \mathrm{n}_1=\mathrm{n}_1+27 \mathrm{x} \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}_1=27 \mathrm{x}$
Substituting this value in equation (i), $\begin{array}{ll} & 152=27 x+11 x \\ \therefore \quad & x=\frac{152}{38}=4$ \end{array}$...(i)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two waves $Y_1=0.25 \sin 316 t$ and $\mathrm{Y}_2=0.25 \sin 310 \mathrm{t}$ are propagating along the same direction. The number of beats produced per second are
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll} & y=A $\sin \omega$ t \\
& $$\text{Given, }$$ y_1=0.25 $\sin 316 $\mathrm{t}$ \\
& $\text{ Comparing$ with (i), } \omega_1=316 \\
& \omega_1=2 \pi $\mathrm{f}_1$ \\
\therefore \quad & $\frac{316}{2 \pi}=$$\mathrm{f}_1$ \\
& $\text{ Given, } \mathrm{y}_2=0.25 \sin 310 $$\mathrm{t}$$ \\
& $\text{ Comparing$ with (i), } \omega_2=310 \\
& \omega_2=2 \pi $$\mathrm{f}_2$$ \\
\therefore \quad & $$\frac{310}{2 \pi}=$$\mathrm{f}_2
\end{array}$ \\ Number of beats produced per second is
$=f_1-f_2=$$\frac{316}{2 \pi}-\frac{310}{2 \pi}=\frac{3}{\pi}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The distance between two consecutive points with phase difference of $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ in wave of frequency 500 Hz is 0.6 m. The velocity with which wave is travelling is
questions.solution:
$\phi=60^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{\pi}{3}$
Path difference is given by, $\begin{array}{ll} \quad \mathrm{x} & =\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \times \phi \\ \therefore \quad 0.6 & =\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \times \frac{\pi}{3} \\ \therefore \quad \lambda & =3.6 \mathrm{ m} \\ \quad v & =\mathrm{n} \lambda=500 \times 3.6=1800 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}=1.8 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{s} \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string A has twice the length, twice the diameter, twice the tension and twice the density of another string B. The overtone of A which will, have the same fundamental frequency as that of B is
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency of string $B$ is,
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}} & =\frac{1}{2 l_{\mathrm{B}}} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{B}}}} \text{. where, } \mu=\text{ mass per unit length. } \\
\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}} & =\rho \pi \mathrm{r}^2 l \\
\therefore \quad \mu_{\mathrm{B}} & =\frac{\rho \pi \mathrm{r}^2 l}{l}=\rho \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \\
\therefore \quad \mu_{\mathrm{A}} & =2 \rho \pi(2 \mathrm{r})^2=8 \mu_{\mathrm{B}} \\
\mu_{\mathrm{A}} & =\frac{8 f \pi \mathrm{r}^2}{2 l}=4 \mu_{\mathrm{B}}
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Fundamental frequency of string A is,
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{2\left(2 l_{\mathrm{B}}\right)} \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{B}}}{8 \mu_{\mathrm{B}}}}=\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2 l_{\mathrm{B}}} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{B}}}}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}$Frequency of $\mathrm{p}^{\text{th }}$ overtone $=(p+1) n$ Here, $(p+1)=4 \Rightarrow p=3\therefore \quad 3^{\text{rd }}$ Overtone of string A will have same frequency as fundamental frequency of string B .

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A progressive wave of frequency 400 Hz is travelling with a velocity $336 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. How far apart are the two points which are $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ out of phase?
questions.solution:
Phase difference $(\phi)=60^{{}^{\circ}}$ or $\frac{\pi}{3} \mathrm{rad}\therefore \quad$ Path difference $=\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \times \phi=\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \times \frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\lambda}{6}\therefore \quad$ Path difference $=\frac{\lambda}{6}=\frac{v}{n} \times \frac{1}{6} \quad \ldots(\because v=\mathrm{n} \lambda)$
Substituting given values,
Path difference $=\frac{336}{400} \times \frac{1}{6}=0.14 \mathrm{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The end correction of resonance tube is 1 cm. If the shortest length resonating with a tuning fork is 15 cm , the next resonating length will be
questions.solution:
Let the shortest length be denoted as $l_1=15.0 \mathrm{ cm}$
The end correction, $\mathrm{e}=1.0 \mathrm{ cm}l_1+\mathrm{e}=\frac{\lambda}{4}$
Now, $l_2+\mathrm{e}=\frac{3 \lambda}{4}\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \frac{l_1+\mathrm{e}}{l_2+\mathrm{e}}=\frac{1}{3} \\ \therefore & \frac{15+1}{l_2+1}=\frac{1}{3} \\ \therefore & l_2+1=48 \\ \therefore & l_2=47 \mathrm{ cm} \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with a velocity of one-fifth of the velocity of sound. The percentage increase in the apparent frequency is
questions.solution:
When observer moves towards the stationary source then apparent frequency, $\mathrmn^{\prime}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathrm{v}}\right) \mathrm{n}$
Given, $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{o}}=\mathrm{v} / 5$. $\therefore \quad \mathrmn^{\prime}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}+\frac{\mathrm{v}}{5}}{\mathrm{v}}\right) \mathrm{n}=\frac{6}{5} \mathrm{n}$
Increase in apparent frequency $=\mathrmn^{\prime}-\mathrm{n}=\frac{6}{5} \mathrm{n}-\mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{5} \mathrm{n} \Rightarrow 20 \%$ of n

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an air column in a pipe open at both ends is ' $\mathrm{f}_1$ '. Now $80 \%$ of its length is immersed in water, the fundamental frequency of the air column becomes $f_2$. The ratio of $f_1: f_2$ is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of the open pipe $=\mathrm{f}_1=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 \dot{\mathrm{ L}}}$
After dipping in water, the pipe behaves like a closed pipe. As the pipe is dipped $80 \%$ in water, $l=\frac{20}{100} \times \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{5}\therefore \quad$ Fundamental frequency $\mathrm{f}_2=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{4 l}=\frac{5 \mathrm{ V}}{4 \mathrm{ L}}\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{f}_1}{\mathrm{f}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{2 \mathrm{ L}} \times \frac{4 \mathrm{ L}}{5 \mathrm{ V}}=\frac{2}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pitch of a whistle of an engine appears to drop by $30 \%$ of original value when it passes a stationary observer. If the speed of sound in air is $350 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, then the speed of engine in $\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ is
questions.solution:
Speed of sound $=350 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ Also,' ....(given) $\mathrmn^{\prime}=\mathrm{n}-\frac{30}{100} \mathrm{n}=\frac{70}{100} \mathrm{n}=0.7 \mathrm{n}$
If $n$ is the original (actual) frequency of the whistle and $\mathrmn^{\prime}$ the frequency as the engine passes the stationary observer, then $\begin{array}{ll} & \frac{\mathrmn^{\prime}}{\mathrm{n}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\text{cngine }}}\right) \\ \therefore \quad & 0.7=\frac{350}{350+\mathrm{v}_{\text{engine }}} \\ & 0.7 \mathrm{y}_{\text{engine }}+245=350 \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{v}_{\text{engine }}=150 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The displacement of a wave is given by $y=0 \cdot 002 \sin (100 t+x)$ where ' $x$ 'and ' $y$ ' are in metre and ' $t$ ' is in second. This represents a wave
options: travelling with a velocity of $100 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ in the negative x -direction
$travelling with a velocity of \left(\frac{50}{\pi}\right) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ in the positive x -direction
questions.solution:
Comparing $\mathrm{y}=0.002 \sin (\omega \mathrm{t}+\mathrm{x})$ with $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{a} \sin$ ( $\omega \mathrm{t}+\mathrm{kx}$ )
We get $\omega=100 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ and $\mathrm{k}=1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{a}=0.002\therefore \quad \mathrm{n}=\frac{\omega}{2 \pi}=\frac{100}{2 \pi}=\frac{50}{\pi} \mathrm{ Hz}$
Velocity $\mathrm{v}=\frac{\omega}{\mathrm{k}}=100 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $\mathrm{k}=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\therefore \quad \lambda=\frac{2 \pi}{\mathrm{k}}=2 \pi \mathrm{ m}$
Thus, it represents a wave travelling with a velocity of $100 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ in the -ve direction.

questions.q: The driver of a car travelling with a speed ' $\mathrm{V}_1$ ' $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ towards a wall sounds a siren of frequency ' $n$ ' Hz. If the velocity of sound in air is ' $V$ ' $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$, then the frequency of the sound reflected from the wall and as heard by the driver in Hz is
questions.solution:
For the source moving towards the wall, $\therefore \quad \mathrm{n}_1=\mathrm{n}\left[\frac{\mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{~V}-\mathrm{V}_1}\right]$
For the reflected sound waves, the driver acts as an observer moving towards the wall $\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_1\left[\frac{\mathrm{~V}+\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}}\right] \\ \therefore & \mathrm{n}_2=\left[\frac{\mathrm{V}+\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}}\right] \times\left[\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}-\mathrm{V}_1}\right] \times \mathrm{n} \\ \therefore & \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}\left[\frac{\mathrm{~V}+\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}-\mathrm{V}_1}\right] \end{array}$

questions.solution: For a string with fixed ends, the length is determined by the number of nodes (x). The length in terms of wavelength is given by $(X+1) \frac{\lambda}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire under tension 225 N produces 6 beats per second when it is tuned with a fork. When the tension changes to 256 N , it is again tuned with the same tuning fork, the number of beats remain unchanged. The frequency of tuning fork will be
questions.solution:
Let n be frequency of tuning fork.
Let $\mathrm{n}_1, \mathrm{n}_2$ be frequency of wire at tension $\mathrm{T}_1, \mathrm{ T}_2$ respectively.
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{n} & \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{ T}}...(i) \\
\mathrm{n}_1 & =\mathrm{n}-6 ...(ii)\\
\mathrm{n}_2 & =\mathrm{n}+6...(iii)
\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \frac{\mathrm{n}_1}{\mathrm{n}_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{ T}_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{225}{256}}=\frac{15}{16} \\
\therefore & \frac{\mathrm{n}-6}{\mathrm{n}+6}=\frac{15}{16}...from(i), (ii),(iii) \\
\therefore & 16 \mathrm{n}-96=15 \mathrm{n}+90 \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{n}=186 \mathrm{ Hz}
\end{array}$

questions.q: Velocity of sound waves in air is $330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. For a particular sound wave in air, path difference of 40 cm is equivalent to phase difference of (1.6) $\pi$. The frequency of this wave is
questions.solution:
Given: $\phi=1.6 \pi$ and $\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{f}}$
We know,
Phase difference $\phi=\frac{2 \pi x}{\lambda}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & 1.6 \pi=\frac{2 \pi x f}{330} \Rightarrow f=\frac{1.6 \times 330}{2 \times 40 \times 0.01} \\ & f=660 \mathrm{ Hz}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Frequency of $\mathrm{n}^{\text{th }}$ harmonic of a closed pipe
$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{nV}}{4 \mathrm{ L}}$Frequency of different modes of vibration in a closed pipe $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{n}^{\prime}=\frac{(2 n-1) \mathrm{V}}{4 \mathrm{ L}_1}\therefore \quad$ Frequency of $2^{\text{nd }}$ overtone, $\mathrm{f}_3^{\prime}=\frac{5 \mathrm{ V}}{4 \mathrm{ L}_1}(\mathrm{n}=3)$
In a closed pipe, the number of nodes and antinodes are the same. Hence, there will be 3 nodes and 3 antinodes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sound waves of frequency $600 \mathrm{ Hz}$ fall normally on a perfectly reflecting wall. The shortest distance from the wall at which all particles will have maximum amplitude of vibration is (speed of sound $=300 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
The maximum displacement of the wave will occur at antinode of the wave. The first antinode will be a point where, $\mathrm{d}=\frac{\lambda}{4}$
The wavelength is given by,
$\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{300}{600}$
So, $d=\frac{0.5}{4}=\frac{1}{8} m$

questions.q:
A wire PQ has length $4.8 \mathrm{ m}$ and mass $0.06 \mathrm{ kg}$. Another wire QR has length $2.56 \mathrm{ m}$ and mass $0.2 \mathrm{ kg}$. Both wires have same radii and are joined as a single wire. This wire is under tension of $80 \mathrm{ N}$. A wave pulse of amplitude $3.5 \mathrm{ cm}$ is sent along the wire $\mathrm{PQ}$ from end $\mathrm{P}$.
The time taken by the wave to reach the other end of single wire is (No power is dissipated during propagation)
questions.solution:
Mass per unit length for wire $P Q$,
$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{PQ}}=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{\mathrm{L}}=\frac{0.06}{4.8}=\frac{1}{80} \mathrm{ kg} / \mathrm{m}$
Similarly for wire $\mathrm{QR}$,
$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{QR}}=\frac{0.2}{2.56}=\frac{5}{64} \mathrm{ kg} / \mathrm{m}\therefore \quad$ Velocity of the wave in PQ wire:
$y=\sqrt{\frac{T}{m_{\mathrm{PQ}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{80}{1 / 80}}=80 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}\therefore \quad$ Time taken to travel PQ wire, $\mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{4.8}{80}=0.06 \mathrm{ s}$ Velocity of wave in QR wire,
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{v} & =\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\text{net }}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{QR}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{(80+0.6) \times 64}{5}} \\
& =32.12 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ Time taken to travel $\mathrm{QR}$ wire, $\mathrm{t}=\frac{2.56}{32.12}=0.08 \mathrm{ s}$
So, total time taken will be:
$\mathrm{t}=0.06+0.08=0.14 \mathrm{ s}$

questions.q: A string is stretched between two rigid supports separated by $75 \mathrm{ cm}$. There are no resonant frequencies between $420 \mathrm{ Hz}$ and $315 \mathrm{ Hz}$. The lowest resonant frequency for the string is
questions.solution:
As there is no resonant frequency between $315 \mathrm{ Hz}$ and $420 \mathrm{ Hz}$, let $315 \mathrm{ Hz}$ be $\mathrmn^{\text{th }}$ overtone and $420 \mathrm{ Hz}$ be $(\mathrm{n}+1)^{\text{th }}$ overtone. Now, $v=\frac{\text{ nv }}{2 l}$
\therefore \quad 315=$\frac{\mathrm{nv}}{2 l} \text{$ and $}420=\frac{(\mathrm{n}+1) \mathrm{v}}{2 l}$ Taking the ratio, $\begin{array}{ll}& \frac{315}{420}=\frac{n}{n+1}$\\
\therefore \quad & 315 n+315=420 n \\
\therefore \quad & n=3
\end{array} The $resonant frequency is v_0=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{2 l}$
Therefore, from equation (i) we get, $v_0=\frac{v}{n}=\frac{315}{3}$=$105 \mathrm{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A progressive wave is given by, $Y=12 \sin (5 t-4 x)$. On this wave, how far away are the two points having a phase difference of $90^{\circ}$ ?
questions.solution:
Given, $y=12 \sin (5 t-4 x)$ $\therefore \quad y=12 \sin 2 \pi\left(\frac{5 t}{2 \pi}-\frac{4 x}{2 \pi}\right)$ 
Comparing above eq. with, 
$\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{A} \sin 2 \pi\left(\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\lambda}-\frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{T}}\right)$
We get, $\lambda=\frac{2 \pi}{4}$
Relation between phase difference and path difference is
$\begin{aligned} \Delta \phi & =\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \Delta \mathrm{x} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\pi}{2} & =\frac{2 \pi}{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{4}\right)} \Delta \mathrm{x} \\ \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{x} & =\frac{\pi}{8}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The equation of the wave is $\mathrm{Y}=10 \sin  \left(\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{t}}{30}+\alpha\right)$ If the displacement is $5 \mathrm{ cm} at  \mathrm{t}=$0$ then the total phase at  \mathrm{t}=$7.5 $\mathrm{ s} will be   \left(\sin30^{{}^{\circ}}=0.5\right)$
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll} & \text{ At } \mathrm{t}=0,10 \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi \times 0}{30}+\alpha\right)=5 \\ \therefore \quad & 10 \sin \alpha=5 \\ \therefore \quad & \sin \alpha=0.5 \\ \therefore \quad & \alpha=\frac{\pi}{6}\end{array}$
Thus, at $\mathrm{t}=$7.5 $\mathrm{ s}$,

10 \sin  $\left(\frac{2 \pi \times 7.5}{30}+\alpha\right)=$10 \sin $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$\therefore \quad$ The total phase is \frac{2 \pi}{3}.$

questions.q: A closed pipe and an open pipe have their first overtone equal in frequency. Then the lengths of these pipes are in the ratio

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{v}}{2 l_{\mathrm{o}}}$
The first overtone for closed pipe is

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equation of a progressive wave is $\mathrm{Y}=\operatorname{asin} 2 \pi \left( n $ t-$\frac{x}{5}\right). The ratio$ of maximum particle velocity of wave velocity is
questions.solution:
The general equation for wave is
$\mathrm{Y}=\mathrm{a} \sin (\omega \mathrm{t}-\mathrm{kx})$
The given equation can be written as
$Y=\operatorname{asin} \left($2 $\pi$n t-2 $\pi \frac{x}{5}\right)
Comparing both equations,
\omega=$2 $\pi$nk=$\frac{2 \pi}{5}
Wave velocity is given as \mathrm{v}=\frac{\omega}{\mathrm{k}}\therefore \quad \mathrm{v}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{n}}{\frac{2 \pi}{5}}=$5 $\mathrm{n}
Particle velocity can be calculated as follows:
\frac{d Y}{d x}=$a(2 $\pi$n) \cos  $\left(2 \pi n t-2 \pi \frac{x}{5}\right)$
Maximum velocity is $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=(2 \pi \mathrm{na})\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{na}}{5 \mathrm{n}}\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{a}}{5}$

questions.q: When two tuning forks are sounded together, 5 beats per second are heard. One of the forks is in unison with $0.97 \mathrm{ m}$ length of sonometer wire and the other is in unison with $0.96 \mathrm{ m}$ length of the same wire. The frequencies of the two tuning forks are
questions.solution:
Given number of beats $=5, l_1=0.97 \mathrm{ m}$, $l_2=0.96 \mathrm{ m}$
The frequencies of the given sonometer are as follows:

If we use another wire 'B' which vibrates with same frequency under tension ' $2 \mathrm{ T}$ ' and diameter ' $2 \mathrm{D}$ ' then density ' $\rho_2$ ' of wire ' $B$ ' will be
questions.solution:
The formula for frequency of a sonometer is $\mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\pi \rho \mathrm{D}^2}}$
Here $l$ is length, $\mathrm{T}$ is tension, $\mathrm{D}$ is diameter and $\rho$ is density.
The frequency of both the wires is same.
The frequency of the wire $\mathrm{A}$ is $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\pi \rho_1 \mathrm{D}^2}}$
The frequency of the wire $\mathrm{B}$ is $f_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{ T}}{\pi \rho_2(2 \mathrm{D})^2}}$
Equating both the frequencies
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\pi \rho \mathrm{D}^2}}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{ T}}{\pi \rho_2(2 \mathrm{D})^2}} \\
& \sqrt{\frac{1}{\rho_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2 \rho_2}} \\
& \frac{1}{\rho_1}=\frac{1}{2 \rho_2} \\
& \therefore \quad \rho_2=\frac{\rho_1}{2}
\end{aligned}$

options: more in the second case than in the first case.
less in the second case than in the first case.
less than the actual frequency in both the cases.
questions.solution:
For observer moving towards a stationary source,
$\mathrm{n}_1=\mathrm{n}_0 \left[\frac{\mathrm{v}+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mathrm{v}}\right]
For source moving towards a stationary observer,
\mathrm{n}}_{2}=\mathrm{n}$}_{0} $\left[\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}}\right]$
Substituting the values for $v, v_L$ and $v_S$ in the equations above
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{n}_1=\mathrm{n}_0\left[\frac{330+50}{330}\right]=1.15 \mathrm{n}_0 \\
& \mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_0\left[\frac{330}{330-50}\right]=1.17 \mathrm{n}_0 \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}_2 \gt \mathrm{n}_1
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad$ The frequency heard will be more in the second case than in the first case.
